title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping
section: Part 1: Practice scraping Books to Scrape
text:
Part 1: Practice scraping Books to Scrape
Turning information displayed on five webpages into one structured dataframe. Each row represents one book listing.

Part 1(a): Run the sample against the practice website

Books to Scrape is designed for scraping practice.
Its static HTML lets us practice extracting information without needing JavaScript tools.
We first read page 1 and inspect the extracted results before repeating the process across more pages.



Part 1(b): Extract titles, prices, and ratings from five pages

We extract each book’s title, price, and star rating.
We convert the price text into a numeric variable called price_gbp.
We repeat the extraction for pages 2–5 and reuse the page 1 results.
We combine the five page-level dataframes into books_all.
The expected result is 100 book listings, with 20 listings from each page.
The additional page column records where each listing came from.

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping
section: Extracting title, price, and rating and binding the scraped data from the first 5 pages into one data frame.
text:
Extracting title, price, and rating and binding the scraped data from the first 5 pages into one data frame.

library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)


## ---- 1. The sandbox: books.toscrape.com ------------------------------------
## Built and published for scraping practice. 1,000 books, 50 pages, no
## JavaScript. Learn the verbs here before you point them at anyone's server.

# Read the first page of book listings
books_pg <- read_html(
  "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-1.html"
)

books <- tibble(
  title  = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |> html_attr("title"),
  price  = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod p.price_color") |> html_text2(),
  rating = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod p.star-rating") |>
             html_attr("class") |> str_remove("star-rating ")
) |>
  mutate(price_gbp = parse_number(price))

head(books)

  title                                 price  rating price_gbp
  <chr>                                 <chr>  <chr>      <dbl>
1 A Light in the Attic                  £51.77 Three       51.8
2 Tipping the Velvet                    £53.74 One         53.7
3 Soumission                            £50.10 One         50.1
4 Sharp Objects                         £47.82 Four        47.8
5 Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind £54.23 Five        54.2
6 The Requiem Red                       £22.65 One         22.7

# Number of rows and columns
dim(books)

[1] 20  4

# Column names and data types
glimpse(books)

Rows: 20

## ----Creating URLs for five pages -----------------------------------------------

books_urls <- paste0("https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-",
                     1:5, ".html")

books_urls

[1] "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-1.html"
[2] "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-2.html"
[3] "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-3.html"
[4] "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-4.html"
[5] "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-5.html"

## ---- Ask permission before fetching ------------------------------------

books_allowed <- robotstxt::paths_allowed(books_urls)

books_allowed

[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE

if (!all(books_allowed %in% TRUE)) {
  stop("Permission was not confirmed for every page.")
}


## ---- Extract five pages ------------------------------------------------

books_list <- list()

# Page 1 was already scraped
books_list[[1]] <- books |>
  mutate(page = 1)

# Scrape pages 2 through 5
for (i in 2:5) {

  Sys.sleep(1)

  books_pg <- read_html(books_urls[i])

  books_page <- tibble(
    title  = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |> html_attr("title"),
    price  = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod p.price_color") |> html_text2(),
    rating = books_pg |> html_elements("article.product_pod p.star-rating") |>
               html_attr("class") |> str_remove("star-rating ")
  ) |>
    mutate(price_gbp = parse_number(price),
           page = i)

  books_list[[i]] <- books_page
}


## ---- Combine the pages -----------------------------------------------

books_all <- bind_rows(books_list)

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping
section: Part 2: Scrape and clean Wikipedia tables
text:
Part 2: Scrape and clean Wikipedia tables
Extracting tables from a real website, adapting the program to another table, and cleaning the results into usable dataframes.

Part 2(a): Scrape the foreign-exchange reserves table

We checked the page’s robots rules before fetching it.
We inspected the candidate tables and extracted the reserves table.
We identified the including-gold amount column: foreign_exchange_reserves.
Its unit is US$ millions.
We retained the country, reserves amount, and reporting date.



Part 2(b): Scrape a different table and explain what changed

We changed the target to Wikipedia’s countries-and-dependencies population table.
The country column changed from country_as_recognized_by_the_un to location.
The amount column changed from foreign_exchange_reserves to population.
The reporting-date column changed from last_reporteddate to date.
Therefore, the column-selection code needed changing.
The reserves table contained two additional header rows that needed removal.
Both tables used day–month–year dates, so the same date-conversion function worked for both.

What broke and why: Column-specific code cannot automatically transfer between tables with different names. The placeholder errors we encountered were caused by unreplaced example names; they were not evidence that Wikipedia had changed its page.


Part 2(c): Clean the dataframes

Standardized column names.
Removed bracketed footnotes, thin spaces, nonbreaking spaces, and extra whitespace.
Removed unnecessary columns.
Removed repeated country headers and any Total or World rows.
Converted reserve amounts and population counts into numbers.
Converted reporting dates into R dates.
Preserved the original amount and date text to check conversions.
Added checks to identify missing or unsuccessfully converted values.

library(robotstxt)
library(lubridate)
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)

World Bank figures are rounded here to whole US$ millions.

Vintage: Wikipedia reports country-specific observations from 2026. The World Bank observations in this comparison are from 2024.
Why they differ: The sources describe different reporting periods. Reserve holdings, exchange rates, and gold valuations can change between those periods.
Rounding, revisions, and methodological differences may also contribute, but the comparison does not establish their individual effects.
Both amounts were converted to US$ millions, so the differences are not simply a dollars-versus-millions mismatch.
India has the largest percentage difference among these four; China has the largest absolute difference.
The World Bank request ended in 2024. This does not establish whether newer observations are available.
These four countries are examples from our displayed output, not necessarily the complete list of differing countries.



Part 3(c): When is scraping the right tool?
Web scraping is the right tool when the required data are available on webpages but cannot be obtained through a suitable API, downloadable dataset, or bulk export. It should be used when the website’s robots rules and Terms of Service permit the intended collection, with reasonable request rates and checks to detect changes in the page structure.

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping
section: Fetch total reserves from the World Bank using one WDI() call.
text:
Fetch total reserves from the World Bank using one WDI() call.

## ---- 3a. The same quantity, from an API ------------------------------------
## Foreign reserves are published by the World Bank as FI.RES.TOTL.CD,
## "Total reserves (includes gold, current US$)".

library(WDI)

reserves_api <- WDI(indicator = "FI.RES.TOTL.CD",
                    start = 2015, end = 2024, extra = TRUE)

## ---- 3b. Prepare World Bank reserves for comparison ------------------------
## Keep countries and economies rather than regional aggregates.
## Convert current US dollars to US$ millions.

reserves_wb <- reserves_api |>
  filter(!is.na(region),
         region != "Aggregates",
         !is.na(FI.RES.TOTL.CD)) |>
  group_by(iso2c) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(country_wb = country,
         iso2c,
         wb_year = year,
         wb_usd = FI.RES.TOTL.CD) |>
  mutate(wb_usd_million = wb_usd / 1000000)

## ---- Match countries and calculate differences ---------------------------

reserves_comparison <- reserves_wiki |>
  left_join(reserves_wb, by = c("country" = "country_wb")) |>
  mutate(difference_million = wiki_usd_million - wb_usd_million,
         difference_percent = if_else(
           !is.na(wb_usd_million) & wb_usd_million != 0,
           100 * difference_million / wb_usd_million,
           NA_real_))

title: Assignment 04_Data Plan
text:
Part 4: Data Acquisition Plan
Research purpose

We will examine whether burglary/breaking and entering, destruction/damage/vandalism of property, motor vehicle theft, and robbery co-locate with recorded drug/narcotic violations and documented homeless encampments in Downtown Dallas and the Harry Hines corridor. We will investigate whether observed patterns also reflect differences in police activity; spatial association alone will not establish causation.

(a) Sources and reasons for choosing them

We will retain three Dallas OpenData datasets: Police Incidents (qv6i-rri7), Police Arrests (sdr7-6v3j), and Dallas Police Active Calls (9fxf-t2tr). They provide complementary information about recorded offenses, arrests, and calls being handled.
Police Incidents will be the main dataset because it contains NIBRS_Crime_Category, which identifies the selected offenses. Arrests and calls will provide additional context about police activity, subject to their coverage and available fields.
We have requested GIS shapefiles for homeless encampments and sexually oriented businesses. We will obtain or define study-area boundaries and check each layer’s observation dates and coordinate system.
We will verify IncidentNum as a linkage field in each table. Because an incident may have multiple offenses, arrests, or call records, We will examine duplicates and summarize related records before joining to avoid inflating counts.

(b) Robots rules and Terms of Service

Before collection, We will check the portal’s robots.txt for the intended paths and review Dallas OpenData’s Terms of Use and dataset-specific licensing. We will record the results and the date checked.
Permission has not yet been verified. We will use only access methods permitted by the applicable rules and terms, follow any attribution requirements, and check restrictions attached to the requested GIS files. A robots check alone does not establish permission for every use.

(c) API availability and scraping justification

The supplied R script uses Socrata API endpoints to retrieve the three datasets as JSON. We will use the API or downloadable exports instead of scraping the displayed tables.
API queries allow filtering and pagination. We will adapt the script’s example filters—August 2020 and sector 640—to the agreed research period and geography; those example settings do not define my study areas.
We will confirm whether Active Calls retains historical records. If it only provides a changing current snapshot, I will request an archive or use it prospectively rather than treating it as a complete historical calls dataset.

(d) Volume, rate limiting, and caching

We will estimate record counts before downloading and retrieve only necessary fields and dates. Pagination will use stable ordering and an endpoint-supported batch size; the script’s 50,000-row setting will be tested.
We will make sequential requests, initially pause one second between batches, use an application token where appropriate, and increase waits after throttling responses. This pause is a proposed collection practice, not a verified portal limit.
We will cache dated raw downloads, metadata, query settings, and cleaned files. Analysis will use cached copies, with controlled refreshes instead of repeated downloads.

(e) Changes and detection

Collection may fail if field names, category labels, endpoints, date formats, coordinates, or identifier conventions change.
We will check required columns, exact offense labels, missing coordinates, date coverage, duplicate identifiers, record counts, and unmatched joins after each download. Unexpected changes will trigger review before analysis.
We will retain original snapshots and document corrections. Spatial and temporal aggregation will use consistent boundaries and periods, including the observation dates of encampment and business locations.

## EPPS 6302
## Assignment 2 - Part A.4(a)
## Website versus gtrendsR: Past five years

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 1. Pull the five-year data using gtrendsR
## ---------------------------------------------------------

r_pull <- gtrends(
  keyword = c("Trump", "Kamala Harris", "Election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

r_df <- r_pull$interest_over_time

# Save the original R data
write_csv(
  r_df,
  "part4a_r_raw.csv"
)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 2. Read the five-year website CSV
## ---------------------------------------------------------

website_df <- read_csv(
  "time_series_US_20210916-1050_20260916-1050_Trump_Kamala Harris_Election_5 year_Gtrend web data.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Remove spaces from column names
names(website_df) <- trimws(names(website_df))

# Rename the first column
names(website_df)[1] <- "date"

View(website_df)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 3. Convert website data from wide to long format
## ---------------------------------------------------------

website_long <- website_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "keyword",
    values_to = "website_hits"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = format(date, "%Y-%m"),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    website_hits = as.numeric(website_hits)
  )

View(website_long)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 4. Prepare the R data
## ---------------------------------------------------------

r_long <- r_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = format(date, "%Y-%m"),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    
    # Replace "<1" with 0.5 so that it is not converted to NA
    r_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

View(r_long)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 5. Convert both datasets to monthly observations
## ---------------------------------------------------------

# The website data are already monthly, but this confirms
# that there is one value per term per month.

website_monthly <- website_long %>%
  group_by(month, keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    website_hits = mean(website_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Average the weekly R observations within each month.

r_monthly <- r_long %>%
  group_by(month, keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    r_hits = mean(r_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 6. Match the website and R observations
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison <- inner_join(
  website_monthly,
  r_monthly,
  by = c("month", "keyword")
) %>%
  mutate(
    difference = r_hits - website_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference),
    
    direction = case_when(
      difference > 0 ~ "R higher",
      difference < 0 ~ "Website higher",
      TRUE ~ "Identical"
    )
  )

View(comparison)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 7. Calculate the differences
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison_summary <- comparison %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    matched_months = n(),
    
    identical_values =
      sum(difference == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    different_values =
      sum(difference != 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_website_value =
      mean(website_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_R_value =
      mean(r_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_difference =
      mean(difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_absolute_difference =
      mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    maximum_absolute_difference =
      max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    general_direction = case_when(
      mean_difference > 0 ~ "R generally higher",
      mean_difference < 0 ~ "Website generally higher",
      TRUE ~ "Same average"
    ),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

comparison_summary


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 8. Confirm that all three terms were matched
## ---------------------------------------------------------

table(comparison$keyword)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 9. Plot the two methods
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison_plot_data <- comparison %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01"))
  ) %>%
  select(
    date,
    keyword,
    website_hits,
    r_hits
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(website_hits, r_hits),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "hits"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    method = recode(
      method,
      website_hits = "Google Trends website",
      r_hits = "gtrendsR"
    )
  )

part4a_plot <- ggplot(
  comparison_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = hits,
    color = method
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ keyword,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Google Trends Website and gtrendsR Comparison",
    subtitle = "United States, Web Search, Past Five Years",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Relative search interest",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

part4a_plot


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 10. Save the outputs
## ---------------------------------------------------------

write_csv(
  website_monthly,
  "part4a_website_monthly.csv"
)

write_csv(
  r_monthly,
  "part4a_r_monthly.csv"
)

write_csv(
  comparison,
  "part4a_comparison.csv"
)

write_csv(
  comparison_summary,
  "part4a_comparison_summary.csv"
)

ggsave(
  filename = "part4a_comparison_plot.png",
  plot = part4a_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 11. Display the saved files
## ---------------------------------------------------------

list.files(
  pattern = "^part4a_",
  full.names = TRUE
)


## 4 Part c)
pull_1 <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

pull_1_df <- pull_1$interest_over_time

write_csv(
  pull_1_df,
  "part4c_pull_1.csv"
)



## Waiting for 2 minutes before running the second block of code

pull_2 <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

pull_2_df <- pull_2$interest_over_time

write_csv(
  pull_2_df,
  "part4c_pull_2.csv"
)


## Comparing the two pulled data 2 minutes apart
pull_1_clean <- pull_1_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    pull_1_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

pull_2_clean <- pull_2_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    pull_2_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

repeated_comparison <- inner_join(
  pull_1_clean,
  pull_2_clean,
  by = c("date", "keyword")
) %>%
  mutate(
    difference = pull_2_hits - pull_1_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  )

View(repeated_comparison)


## Comparison Summary

repeated_summary <- repeated_comparison %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    matched_observations = n(),
    identical_values =
      sum(difference == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    different_values =
      sum(difference != 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_difference =
      mean(difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_absolute_difference =
      mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum_absolute_difference =
      max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

repeated_summary


write_csv(
  repeated_comparison,
  "part4c_repeated_comparison.csv"
)

write_csv(
  repeated_summary,
  "part4c_repeated_summary.csv"
)

  "time_series_US_20210916-1050_20260916-1050_Trump_Kamala Harris_Election_5 year_Gtrend web data.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Remove spaces from column names
names(website_df) <- trimws(names(website_df))

# Rename the first column
names(website_df)[1] <- "date"

View(website_df)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 3. Convert website data from wide to long format
## ---------------------------------------------------------

website_long <- website_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "keyword",
    values_to = "website_hits"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = format(date, "%Y-%m"),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    website_hits = as.numeric(website_hits)
  )

View(website_long)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 4. Prepare the R data
## ---------------------------------------------------------

r_long <- r_df %>%
  transmute(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = format(date, "%Y-%m"),
    keyword = tolower(trimws(keyword)),
    
    # Replace "<1" with 0.5 so that it is not converted to NA
    r_hits = ifelse(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      as.numeric(as.character(hits))
    )
  )

View(r_long)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 5. Convert both datasets to monthly observations
## ---------------------------------------------------------

# The website data are already monthly, but this confirms
# that there is one value per term per month.

website_monthly <- website_long %>%
  group_by(month, keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    website_hits = mean(website_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Average the weekly R observations within each month.

r_monthly <- r_long %>%
  group_by(month, keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    r_hits = mean(r_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 6. Match the website and R observations
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison <- inner_join(
  website_monthly,
  r_monthly,
  by = c("month", "keyword")
) %>%
  mutate(
    difference = r_hits - website_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference),
    
    direction = case_when(
      difference > 0 ~ "R higher",
      difference < 0 ~ "Website higher",
      TRUE ~ "Identical"
    )
  )

View(comparison)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 7. Calculate the differences
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison_summary <- comparison %>%
  group_by(keyword) %>%
  summarise(
    matched_months = n(),
    
    identical_values =
      sum(difference == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    different_values =
      sum(difference != 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_website_value =
      mean(website_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_R_value =
      mean(r_hits, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_difference =
      mean(difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_absolute_difference =
      mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    maximum_absolute_difference =
      max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    general_direction = case_when(
      mean_difference > 0 ~ "R generally higher",
      mean_difference < 0 ~ "Website generally higher",
      TRUE ~ "Same average"
    ),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

comparison_summary


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 8. Confirm that all three terms were matched
## ---------------------------------------------------------

table(comparison$keyword)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 9. Plot the two methods
## ---------------------------------------------------------

comparison_plot_data <- comparison %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01"))
  ) %>%
  select(
    date,
    keyword,
    website_hits,
    r_hits
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(website_hits, r_hits),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "hits"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    method = recode(
      method,
      website_hits = "Google Trends website",
      r_hits = "gtrendsR"
    )
  )

part4a_plot <- ggplot(
  comparison_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = hits,
    color = method
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ keyword,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Google Trends Website and gtrendsR Comparison",
    subtitle = "United States, Web Search, Past Five Years",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Relative search interest",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

part4a_plot


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 10. Save the outputs
## ---------------------------------------------------------

write_csv(
  website_monthly,
  "part4a_website_monthly.csv"
)

write_csv(
  r_monthly,
  "part4a_r_monthly.csv"
)

write_csv(
  comparison,
  "part4a_comparison.csv"
)

write_csv(
  comparison_summary,
  "part4a_comparison_summary.csv"
)

ggsave(
  filename = "part4a_comparison_plot.png",
  plot = part4a_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)


## ---------------------------------------------------------
## 11. Display the saved files
## ---------------------------------------------------------

list.files(
  pattern = "^part4a_",
  full.names = TRUE
)

section: Part 3: Download the data and calculate the poverty rate
text:
Part 3: Download the data and calculate the poverty rate

This chunk downloads the 2024 ACS estimates, margins of error, and geographic boundaries for Texas counties. The E suffix identifies an estimate, while the M suffix identifies its margin of error. It then calculates the poverty rate and propagates the uncertainty using moe_prop().

# Download the selected ACS variables and Texas county geometry
# Wide output produces one row per county with separate estimate and MOE columns
acs_wide <- get_acs(
    geography = geo_level,  # Use counties as the geographic unit
    variables = my_vars,    # Download the three selected ACS variables
    state = state_abbr,     # Limit the data to Texas
    year = year_acs,        # Use the 2024 ACS
    survey = survey,        # Use the ACS 5-year estimates
    geometry = TRUE,        # Retain county boundaries for mapping
    output = "wide"         # Produce one row for each county
)

# Derive the poverty rate and carry its margin of error through
acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
    mutate(
        pov_rate = povE / povdenE, # Divide poverty count by its denominator
        pov_moe = moe_prop(        # Calculate the MOE for the poverty rate
            povE,                  # Poverty-count estimate
            povdenE,               # Poverty-denominator estimate
            povM,                  # MOE for the poverty-count estimate
            povdenM                # MOE for the denominator estimate
        )
    )

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(a) Map Interpretation
The map shows substantial variation in median household income across Texas counties. Higher-income counties appear primarily around major metropolitan areas, especially the Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin, and Houston regions. Many counties in South Texas, along the Rio Grande border, and in parts of West Texas have lower median household incomes. Overall, the pattern suggests that counties near large urban economies tend to have higher household incomes than many rural and border counties.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(b) Table Interpretation
The highest estimated poverty rate is in Dimmit County at approximately 41.1%, followed by Zapata County at 38.4% and Zavala County at 33.9%. Many counties in the highest-poverty group are located in South Texas or near the Texas–Mexico border. In contrast, Rockwall County has the lowest estimated poverty rate at approximately 4.0%, followed by Sterling County at 4.3% and Sutton County at 4.5%. The margins of error vary substantially across counties, meaning the estimated ordering should be interpreted cautiously, particularly for counties with relatively large margins of error.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(c) Uncertainty Check
Dimmit County and Zapata County provide one clear example of overlapping confidence intervals.

Dimmit County: estimated poverty rate = 41.1%, MOE = 8.9 percentage points, interval = 32.2%–50.0%.
Zapata County: estimated poverty rate = 38.4%, MOE = 6.0 percentage points, interval = 32.4%–44.4%.

The two intervals overlap substantially. Therefore, although Dimmit County is ranked above Zapata County based on the point estimates, the data do not provide strong evidence that Dimmit County’s true poverty rate is higher. Sampling uncertainty could reverse or eliminate the apparent difference. The ranking should consequently be treated as descriptive rather than as a definitive ordering of the counties.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4(d) Methods Note
This analysis uses 2024 American Community Survey five-year estimates for Texas counties. Counties were selected because they provide meaningful geographic comparisons while remaining readable on a statewide map. Median household income (B19013_001) was mapped to show the geographic distribution of economic resources. Poverty was measured using the population below the poverty level (B17001_002) divided by the population for whom poverty status was determined (B17001_001). Using a rate instead of a raw count prevents counties with larger populations from appearing more disadvantaged simply because they contain more residents. I retained the ACS margins of error and used moe_prop() to propagate uncertainty into the calculated poverty rate. The margins of error show that some county estimates are much less precise than others. Several confidence intervals overlap, so small differences between counties should not be interpreted as definitive differences in their true poverty rates. Consequently, the top-and-bottom rankings are descriptive and should be interpreted cautiously.

The website CSV gave me only the interest_over_time data. It did not give me the interest_by_country, interest_by_region, interest_by_dma, interest_by_city, related_topics, or related_queries data frames. Because onlyInterest was left at its default value, gtrendsR returned these additional data frames in the tct object.
No, the “Harris” and “Kamala Harris” series are not the same. Their values and patterns differ because Google treats them as two different search terms. “Kamala Harris” captures searches containing the full name, while “Harris” captures searches for the word “Harris,” which may refer to Kamala Harris or to unrelated people, places, and organizations.
The gap shows that a search term is not necessarily the same as the concept the researcher wants to measure. The search term “Harris” is broad and ambiguous because it can capture searches unrelated to Kamala Harris. Therefore, it has lower measurement validity as an indicator of public interest in Kamala Harris. The more specific term “Kamala Harris” provides a closer measure of the intended concept, although it may still miss searches using other wording. Researchers must carefully choose search terms and explain how those terms operationalize the concept they intend to study.
For Trump, the website values were approximately 7.59 points higher on average, with a maximum difference of 28.50 points. Kamala Harris showed a much smaller difference: the R values were approximately 0.10 points higher on average, although the mean absolute difference was 0.78 points and the maximum difference was 5.50 points. Thus, the direction was not uniform across all terms: the website was generally higher for Trump and election, while R was slightly higher on average for Kamala Harris.

title: Assignment 2 Notes
section: Nevertheless, this result does not mean Google Trends data are permanently fixed or completely reproducible. Google Trends uses a sample of searches and normalizes the results according to the selected terms, geography, and time period. The identical results may mean that Google returned the same sample or a cached version of the data during the short interval between my calls. A query repeated later could still produce different values. Therefore, every finding reported from Google Trends should be treated as an estimate of relative search interest rather than an exact count. Researchers should record the complete query parameters and retrieval time, save the original data, and repeat important queries to test whether their substantive conclusions remain stable. Small differences should not be overinterpreted, even though the two pulls in this particular test were identical.

library(ggdag)

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
What is causal inference?
Causal inference asks not “are X and Y correlated” but “if I intervened and changed X, would Y change as a result” — it’s the toolkit for answering that under real-world data limitations, not just experiments.

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
Research question
What organizational characteristics cause a terrorist organization to be more lethal? (Asal & Rethemeyer 2008)

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
Build the DAG

dag <- dagify(
  L  ~ I + Sz + SS + Ag + C + T + R + W,   # Lethality caused by all these
  T  ~ R,                                   # Regime type -> territorial control
  C  ~ Sz,                                  # Size -> alliance connections
  D  ~ I + Sz,                              # Selection into dataset (the collider)
  exposure = "T",
  outcome  = "L",
  labels = c(
    I  = "Ideology",
    Sz = "Org Size",
    SS = "State\nSponsorship",
    Ag = "Org Age",
    C  = "Alliance\nConnections",
    T  = "Territorial\nControl",
    R  = "Regime\nType",
    W  = "Wealth",
    D  = "Dataset\nSelection",
    L  = "Lethality"
  )
)

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
Basic diagram

ggdag(dag, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  ggtitle("Asal & Rethemeyer (2008): Organizational Lethality DAG")

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
section: Confounder check: paths between Territorial Control and Lethality
text:
Confounder check: paths between Territorial Control and Lethality
Regime Type (R) is a common cause of both Territorial Control (T) and Lethality (L) directly, creating a backdoor path T <- R -> L.

ggdag_paths(dag, from = "T", to = "L", text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  ggtitle("Open paths between Territorial Control and Lethality")

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
Required adjustment set
This computes, from the DAG structure, which variables must be controlled for to identify the causal effect of Territorial Control on Lethality.

ggdag_adjustment_set(dag, exposure = "T", outcome = "L",
                      text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  ggtitle("Adjustment set to identify effect of Territorial Control on Lethality")

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
Collider check
D (whether an organization appears in the TKB dataset at all) is caused by both Ideology and Size — a collider created by sample selection, since TKB only contains organizations that already committed a violent act.

ggdag_collider(dag, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  ggtitle("Collider check")

title: Causal Structure of Organizational Lethality
text:
Notes

Confounder (Regime Type): must be adjusted for — it is a common cause of Territorial Control and Lethality.
Collider (Dataset Selection): must NOT be adjusted for. Because TKB only includes organizations that already used violence, the entire study is structurally conditioned on this collider — a limitation Asal & Rethemeyer acknowledge directly, noting that unclaimed/nonviolent religious organizations are systematically absent from the sample.

      log1p(

  target_category ~
    ideology_factor * OCI_factor_z +

    link = "logit"
  ),

  control = lme4::glmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(
      maxfun = 200000
    )
  )
)

## 6. Multicollinearity diagnostics


#| label: component-vif

calculate_vif <- function(variable, data, predictors) {

  other_predictors <- setdiff(
    predictors,
    variable
  )

  auxiliary_formula <- as.formula(
    paste(
      variable,
      "~",
      paste(other_predictors, collapse = " + ")
    )
  )

  auxiliary_model <- lm(
    auxiliary_formula,
    data = data
  )

  auxiliary_r_squared <- summary(
    auxiliary_model
  )$r.squared

  vif_value <- 1 / (1 - auxiliary_r_squared)

  data.frame(
    Variable = variable,
    Auxiliary_R2 = auxiliary_r_squared,
    VIF = vif_value,
    Tolerance = 1 / vif_value
  )
}

## 6. Function for estimating Model 2

#| label: estimation-function

estimate_loo_model <- function(
  data,
  index_variable,
  model_label
) {

  analysis_data <- data |>
    mutate(
      loo_oci = .data[[index_variable]]
    )

  cat(
    "\nEstimating:",
    model_label,
    "\n"
  )

  starting_time <- Sys.time()

  fitted_model <- glmer(
    hard_target ~
      ideology * loo_oci +
      conflict_region +
      ln_lagged_district_intensity +
      year +
      (1 | organization),

    data = analysis_data,

    family = binomial(
      link = "logit"
    ),

    # Faster approximation for the initial run
    nAGQ = 0,

    control = glmerControl(
      optimizer = "bobyqa",

      optCtrl = list(
        maxfun = 100000
      ),

      calc.derivs = FALSE
    )
  )

  ending_time <- Sys.time()

  cat(
    "Completed:",
    model_label,
    "\n"
  )

  cat(
    "Estimation time:",
    round(
      as.numeric(
        difftime(
          ending_time,
          starting_time,
          units = "mins"
        )
      ),
      2
    ),
    "minutes\n"
  )

  return(fitted_model)
}

## 7. Estimate the four leave-one-component-out models

  safe_file_name <- paste0(
    "model_",
    gsub(
      pattern = "[^A-Za-z0-9]+",
      replacement = "_",
      x = tolower(current_label)
    ),
    ".rds"
  )

  current_model_file <- file.path(
    output_directory,
    safe_file_name
  )

  if (file.exists(current_model_file)) {

    cat(
      "\nLoading saved model:",
      current_label,
      "\n"
    )

    loo_models[[current_label]] <-
      readRDS(current_model_file)

  } else {

    loo_models[[current_label]] <-
      estimate_loo_model(
        data = model_data,
        index_variable = current_variable,
        model_label = current_label
      )

    saveRDS(
      loo_models[[current_label]],
      current_model_file
    )

    cat(
      "Saved completed model to:",
      current_model_file,

    )

    mutate(
      Model = model_label,

      Predictor = recode(
        term,

        "ideologySeparatist/Ethnonationalist:loo_oci" =
          "Separatist × OCI",

        "ideologyIslamist:loo_oci" =

      ),

      Odds_Ratio =
        exp(estimate),

      OR_CI_Lower =
        exp(conf.low),

      OR_CI_Upper =
        exp(conf.high)
    ) |>
    select(
      Model,
      Predictor,
      Coefficient = estimate,
      `Standard Error` = std.error,

## 9. Calculate ideology-specific OCI slopes

#| label: ideology-specific-slopes

extract_slopes <- function(
  fitted_model,
  model_label
) {

  trend_results <- emtrends(
    fitted_model,
    specs = ~ ideology,
    var = "loo_oci"
  )

  trend_table <- as.data.frame(
    summary(
      trend_results,
      infer = c(TRUE, TRUE),
      level = 0.95
    )
  )

  # Identify the confidence-interval column names
  lower_column <- intersect(
    c("asymp.LCL", "lower.CL"),
    names(trend_table)
  )[1]

  upper_column <- intersect(
    c("asymp.UCL", "upper.CL"),
    names(trend_table)
  )[1]

  if (
    is.na(lower_column) ||
    is.na(upper_column)
  ) {
    stop(
      paste(
        "Confidence-interval columns could not",
        "be identified in the emtrends output."
      )
    )
  }

  trend_table |>
    mutate(
      Model = model_label,

      CI_Lower =
        .data[[lower_column]],

      CI_Upper =
        .data[[upper_column]]
    ) |>
    transmute(
      Model,

      Ideology =
        ideology,

      `OCI Slope` =
        loo_oci.trend,

      `Standard Error` =
        SE,

      `95% CI Lower` =
        CI_Lower,

      `95% CI Upper` =
        CI_Upper,

      `p-value` =
        p.value
    )
}

## 11. Extract model diagnostics


#| label: diagnostics-function

extract_model_diagnostics <- function(
  fitted_model,
  model_label
) {

  random_variance <- as.data.frame(
    VarCorr(fitted_model)
  )$vcov[1]

  random_sd <-
    sqrt(random_variance)

  icc <- random_variance /
    (
      random_variance +
      (pi^2 / 3)
    )

  optimizer_code <-
    fitted_model@optinfo$conv$opt

  convergence_messages <-
    fitted_model@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages

  data.frame(
    Model = model_label,

    Observations =
      nobs(fitted_model),

    Organizations =
      length(
        unique(
          fitted_model@frame$organization
        )
      ),

    Log_Likelihood =
      as.numeric(
        logLik(fitted_model)
      ),

    AIC =
      AIC(fitted_model),

    BIC =
      BIC(fitted_model),

    Random_Intercept_Variance =
      random_variance,

    Random_Intercept_SD =
      random_sd,

    ICC =
      icc,

    Singular =
      isSingular(
        fitted_model,
        tol = 0.0001
      ),

    Optimizer_Code =
      paste(
        optimizer_code,
        collapse = ", "
      ),

    Convergence_Warnings =
      ifelse(
        is.null(convergence_messages),
        "None",
        paste(
          convergence_messages,
          collapse = "; "
        )
      )
  )
}

## Function that constructs an OCI window


#| label: oci-construction-function

construct_oci <- function(data, window_length) {

  organization_years <- data |>
    distinct(gname, iyear) |>
    arrange(gname, iyear)

  calculate_one_year <- function(group_name, focal_year) {

    historical_data <- data |>
      filter(
        gname == group_name,
        iyear >= focal_year - window_length,
        iyear <= focal_year - 1
      )

    prior_attacks <- nrow(historical_data)

    if (prior_attacks == 0) {
      return(
        data.frame(
          gname = group_name,
          iyear = focal_year,
          prior_attacks = NA_real_,
          tactical_diversity = NA_real_,
          geographic_spread = NA_real_,
          adjusted_success_rate = NA_real_
        )
      )
    }

    # Exclude GTD attack type 9, which is Unknown
    known_tactics <- historical_data |>
      filter(
        !is.na(attacktype1),
        attacktype1 != 9
      )

    if (nrow(known_tactics) == 0) {

      tactical_diversity <- NA_real_

    } else {

      tactic_counts <- table(
        known_tactics$attacktype1
      )

      tactic_proportions <-
        as.numeric(tactic_counts) /
        sum(tactic_counts)

      shannon_entropy <- -sum(
        tactic_proportions *
          log(tactic_proportions)
      )

      # Eight known GTD attack categories
      tactical_diversity <-
        shannon_entropy / log(8)
    }

    geographic_spread <- n_distinct(
      historical_data$district_spatial,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

    if (geographic_spread == 0) {
      geographic_spread <- NA_real_
    }

    number_successful <- sum(
      historical_data$success == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

    adjusted_success_rate <-
      (number_successful + 1) /
      (prior_attacks + 2)

    data.frame(
      gname = group_name,
      iyear = focal_year,
      prior_attacks = prior_attacks,
      tactical_diversity = tactical_diversity,
      geographic_spread = geographic_spread,
      adjusted_success_rate =
        adjusted_success_rate
    )
  }

  component_rows <- vector(
    mode = "list",
    length = nrow(organization_years)
  )

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(organization_years))) {

    component_rows[[i]] <- calculate_one_year(
      group_name =
        organization_years$gname[i],

      focal_year =
        organization_years$iyear[i]
    )
  }

  components <- bind_rows(component_rows) |>
    filter(
      if_all(
        c(
          prior_attacks,
          tactical_diversity,
          geographic_spread,
          adjusted_success_rate
        ),
        ~ !is.na(.x)
      )
    ) |>
    mutate(
      ln_prior_attacks =
        log1p(prior_attacks),

      ln_geographic_spread =
        log1p(geographic_spread),

      z_prior_attacks =
        as.numeric(scale(ln_prior_attacks)),

      z_tactical_diversity =
        as.numeric(scale(tactical_diversity)),

      z_geographic_spread =
        as.numeric(scale(ln_geographic_spread)),

      z_success_rate =
        as.numeric(scale(adjusted_success_rate)),

      OCI = rowMeans(
        cbind(
          z_prior_attacks,
          z_tactical_diversity,
          z_geographic_spread,
          z_success_rate
        )
      ),

      window = window_length
    )

  return(components)
}

#| label: window-model-function

estimate_window_model <- function(
  data,
  oci_variable,
  model_label
) {

  model_data <- data |>
    mutate(
      OCI_window =
        .data[[oci_variable]]
    )

  fitted_model <- glmer(
    hard_target ~
      ideology * OCI_window +
      conflict_region +
      ln_lagged_district_intensity +
      year +
      (1 | organization),

    data = model_data,

    family = binomial(
      link = "logit"
    ),

    # Fast initial estimation
    nAGQ = 0,

    control = glmerControl(
      optimizer = "bobyqa",

      optCtrl = list(
        maxfun = 100000
      ),

      calc.derivs = FALSE
    )
  )

  return(fitted_model)
}

## Function that constructs an OCI window


#| label: oci-construction-function

construct_oci <- function(data, window_length) {

  organization_years <- data |>
    distinct(gname, iyear) |>
    arrange(gname, iyear)

  calculate_one_year <- function(group_name, focal_year) {

    historical_data <- data |>
      filter(
        gname == group_name,
        iyear >= focal_year - window_length,
        iyear <= focal_year - 1
      )

    prior_attacks <- nrow(historical_data)

    if (prior_attacks == 0) {
      return(
        data.frame(
          gname = group_name,
          iyear = focal_year,
          prior_attacks = NA_real_,
          tactical_diversity = NA_real_,
          geographic_spread = NA_real_,
          adjusted_success_rate = NA_real_
        )
      )
    }

    # Exclude GTD attack type 9, which is Unknown
    known_tactics <- historical_data |>
      filter(
        !is.na(attacktype1),
        attacktype1 != 9
      )

    if (nrow(known_tactics) == 0) {

      tactical_diversity <- NA_real_

    } else {

      tactic_counts <- table(
        known_tactics$attacktype1
      )

      tactic_proportions <-
        as.numeric(tactic_counts) /
        sum(tactic_counts)

      shannon_entropy <- -sum(
        tactic_proportions *
          log(tactic_proportions)
      )

      # Eight known GTD attack categories
      tactical_diversity <-
        shannon_entropy / log(8)
    }

    geographic_spread <- n_distinct(
      historical_data$district_spatial,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

    if (geographic_spread == 0) {
      geographic_spread <- NA_real_
    }

    number_successful <- sum(
      historical_data$success == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

    adjusted_success_rate <-
      (number_successful + 1) /
      (prior_attacks + 2)

    data.frame(
      gname = group_name,
      iyear = focal_year,
      prior_attacks = prior_attacks,
      tactical_diversity = tactical_diversity,
      geographic_spread = geographic_spread,
      adjusted_success_rate =
        adjusted_success_rate
    )
  }

  component_rows <- vector(
    mode = "list",
    length = nrow(organization_years)
  )

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(organization_years))) {

    component_rows[[i]] <- calculate_one_year(
      group_name =
        organization_years$gname[i],

      focal_year =
        organization_years$iyear[i]
    )
  }

  components <- bind_rows(component_rows) |>
    filter(
      if_all(
        c(
          prior_attacks,
          tactical_diversity,
          geographic_spread,
          adjusted_success_rate
        ),
        ~ !is.na(.x)
      )
    ) |>
    mutate(
      ln_prior_attacks =
        log1p(prior_attacks),

      ln_geographic_spread =
        log1p(geographic_spread),

      z_prior_attacks =
        as.numeric(scale(ln_prior_attacks)),

      z_tactical_diversity =
        as.numeric(scale(tactical_diversity)),

      z_geographic_spread =
        as.numeric(scale(ln_geographic_spread)),

      z_success_rate =
        as.numeric(scale(adjusted_success_rate)),

      OCI = rowMeans(
        cbind(
          z_prior_attacks,
          z_tactical_diversity,
          z_geographic_spread,
          z_success_rate
        )
      ),

      window = window_length
    )

  return(components)
}

#| label: window-model-function

estimate_window_model <- function(

      optimizer = "bobyqa",

        maxfun = 100000

    )
  )

}

## Prepare each analytical sample

#| label: prepare-model-data

prepare_target_sample <- function(
  data,
  outcome_variable
) {

  data |>
    filter(
      ideology_category %in% c(
        "Maoist",
        "Separatist/Ethnonationalist",
        "Islamist"
      ),
      !is.na(OCI)
    ) |>
    transmute(
      hard_target =
        as.numeric(
          .data[[outcome_variable]]
        ),

      organization =
        factor(gname),

      organization_year =
        interaction(
          gname,
          iyear,
          drop = TRUE
        ),

      year =
        factor(iyear),

      ideology = factor(
        ideology_category,
        levels = c(
          "Maoist",
          "Separatist/Ethnonationalist",
          "Islamist"
        )
      ),

      conflict_region = factor(
        conflict_region,
        levels = c(
          "Rest of India",
          "Kashmir",
          "Maoist-affected belt",
          "Northeast"
        )
      ),

      OCI =
        as.numeric(OCI),

      ln_lagged_district_intensity =
        log1p(
          as.numeric(
            lagged_district_terrorism_intensity
          )
        )
    ) |>
    filter(
      if_all(
        everything(),
        ~ !is.na(.x)
      )
    )
}

narrow_sample <- prepare_target_sample(
  target_data,
  "target_narrow"
)

#| label: target-sample-summary

    Hard_Targets =
      sum(data$hard_target == 1),

    Soft_Targets =
      sum(data$hard_target == 0),

    Percent_Hard =
      100 * mean(data$hard_target == 1)
  )
}

## Estimate Model 2

#| label: target-model-function

estimate_target_model <- function(data) {

  glmer(
    hard_target ~
      ideology * OCI +
      conflict_region +
      ln_lagged_district_intensity +
      year +
      (1 | organization),

    data = data,

    family = binomial(
      link = "logit"
    ),

    # Faster initial analysis
    nAGQ = 0,

    control = glmerControl(
      optimizer = "bobyqa",

      optCtrl = list(
        maxfun = 100000
      ),

      calc.derivs = FALSE
    )
  )
}



#| label: estimate-target-models

target_output_directory <-
  "robustness_3_target_outputs"

if (!dir.exists(target_output_directory)) {
  dir.create(target_output_directory)
}

target_models <- list()

target_samples <- list(
  "Narrow definition" =
    narrow_sample,

  "Broad definition excluding Unknown" =
    broad_sample
)

for (model_name in names(target_samples)) {

  safe_name <- paste0(
    "model_",
    gsub(
      "[^A-Za-z0-9]+",
      "_",
      tolower(model_name)
    ),
    ".rds"
  )

  model_path <- file.path(
    target_output_directory,
    safe_name
  )

  if (file.exists(model_path)) {

    cat(
      "Loading:",
      model_name,
      "\n"
    )

    target_models[[model_name]] <-
      readRDS(model_path)

  } else {

    cat(
      "Estimating:",
      model_name,
      "\n"
    )

    target_models[[model_name]] <-
      estimate_target_model(
        target_samples[[model_name]]
      )

    saveRDS(
      target_models[[model_name]],
      model_path
    )
  }
}

## Average predicted probabilities

## This uses empirical averaging over the observed covariate distributions.


#| label: average-predictions

calculate_average_predictions <- function(
  model,
  data,
  model_label
) {

  oci_grid <- seq(
    quantile(
      data$OCI,
      0.025,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    quantile(
      data$OCI,
      0.975,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    length.out = 15
  )

  prediction_results <- avg_predictions(
    model,

    newdata = datagrid(
      model = model,
      grid_type = "counterfactual",
      OCI = oci_grid,
      ideology = levels(data$ideology)
    ),

    by = c(
      "ideology",
      "OCI"
    ),

    re.form = NA
  )

  as.data.frame(prediction_results) |>
    mutate(
      Model = model_label
    )
}

## Function to download PDFs

download_govfiles_pdf <- function(url, id) {
  tryCatch({
    destfile <- paste0(save_dir, "govfiles_", id, ".pdf")

    status <- download.file(
      url,
      destfile = destfile,
      mode = "wb"
    )

    if (status != 0) {
      stop("Download failed")
    }

    # Check that the downloaded file has a PDF header
    pdf_header <- readBin(destfile, what = "raw", n = 5)

    if (!identical(pdf_header, charToRaw("%PDF-"))) {
      stop("Downloaded file is not a PDF")
    }

    Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))

    return(paste("Successfully downloaded:", id))
  },
  error = function(e) {
    return(paste("Failed to download:", id))
  })
}

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
text:
Step 4 : Report

Difficulties encountered
I downloaded the ten most recent Senate Committee on Foreign Relations hearings available through the refined GovInfo search, including subcommittee hearings, using both a website CSV export and API search results. Both methods successfully downloaded ten PDFs and returned the same ten hearings in the same order.
The initial phrase search also returned a hearing issued by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation because it mentioned Foreign Relations. I addressed this by restricting the search to the Senate chamber and the Foreign Relations committee. I also encountered an R error when combining API results because some fields contained nested lists of unequal lengths. Extracting simple fields before combining the records resolved this problem. Another error occurred when combining download logs before the CSV log object had been created; creating the missing log resolved it.


a. Usability of the documents as data
The PDFs provide source documents for analysis, but downloading them does not automatically produce an analysis-ready dataset. Their text must first be extracted and checked for completeness. Any scanned pages without usable embedded text would require optical character recognition (OCR). Headers, footers, page numbers, and formatting may also require cleaning, while tables and images may need separate processing.
To create a document-level table, I would use one row per hearing and include its package ID, title, date, committee, and document link. To create a text corpus, I would extract each hearing’s text, associate it with its package ID, and check the extraction against the original PDF. Analysis of individual statements would require additional work to identify speakers and separate their testimony.


b. Improvements to the process
I would use committee and chamber metadata filters from the beginning rather than relying only on a phrase search. I would also examine the available HTML or text versions before extracting text from PDFs, since these formats may simplify text processing. The PDFs would remain useful for checking the original layout, tables, and images.
Metadata can supply identifiers, titles, dates, committee information, and available download links without manually opening each hearing. I would preserve this metadata alongside the download log, record the query and sorting settings, and add retries for failed requests. If collecting more documents, I would use pagination to retrieve additional results.


c. What the API added
The API provided structured search results and document metadata that R could retrieve directly, reducing the manual exporting and page parsing required by website searches and scraping. It also supported repeatable requests with specified queries, sorting, and pagination, making the collection process easier to document and rerun.

## Function to download PDFs

download_govfiles_pdf <- function(url, id) {
  tryCatch({
    destfile <- paste0(save_dir, "govfiles_", id, ".pdf")

    status <- download.file(
      url,
      destfile = destfile,
      mode = "wb"
    )

    if (status != 0) {
      stop("Download failed")
    }

    # Check that the downloaded file has a PDF header
    pdf_header <- readBin(destfile, what = "raw", n = 5)

    if (!identical(pdf_header, charToRaw("%PDF-"))) {
      stop("Downloaded file is not a PDF")
    }

    Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))

    return(paste("Successfully downloaded:", id))
  },
  error = function(e) {
    return(paste("Failed to download:", id))
  })
}

text:
Step 4 : Report

Difficulties encountered
I downloaded the ten most recent Senate Committee on Foreign Relations hearings available through the refined GovInfo search, including subcommittee hearings, using both a website CSV export and API search results. Both methods successfully downloaded ten PDFs and returned the same ten hearings in the same order.
The initial phrase search also returned a hearing issued by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation because it mentioned Foreign Relations. I addressed this by restricting the search to the Senate chamber and the Foreign Relations committee. I also encountered an R error when combining API results because some fields contained nested lists of unequal lengths. Extracting simple fields before combining the records resolved this problem. Another error occurred when combining download logs before the CSV log object had been created; creating the missing log resolved it.


a. Usability of the documents as data
The PDFs provide source documents for analysis, but downloading them does not automatically produce an analysis-ready dataset. Their text must first be extracted and checked for completeness. Any scanned pages without usable embedded text would require optical character recognition (OCR). Headers, footers, page numbers, and formatting may also require cleaning, while tables and images may need separate processing.
To create a document-level table, I would use one row per hearing and include its package ID, title, date, committee, and document link. To create a text corpus, I would extract each hearing’s text, associate it with its package ID, and check the extraction against the original PDF. Analysis of individual statements would require additional work to identify speakers and separate their testimony.


b. Improvements to the process
I would use committee and chamber metadata filters from the beginning rather than relying only on a phrase search. I would also examine the available HTML or text versions before extracting text from PDFs, since these formats may simplify text processing. The PDFs would remain useful for checking the original layout, tables, and images.
Metadata can supply identifiers, titles, dates, committee information, and available download links without manually opening each hearing. I would preserve this metadata alongside the download log, record the query and sorting settings, and add retries for failed requests. If collecting more documents, I would use pagination to retrieve additional results.


c. What the API added
The API provided structured search results and document metadata that R could retrieve directly, reducing the manual exporting and page parsing required by website searches and scraping. It also supported repeatable requests with specified queries, sorting, and pagination, making the collection process easier to document and rerun.
